raw_response:
I'm 50 years old, been farming these fields in Quzhou since I was young. Didn't study much — only primary school — but I know my land. My family has about 10 mu. Last year the wheat did fine, got around 1000 jin per mu. My neighbor Old Wang, he's about my age, farms 8 mu of wheat-maize and 2 mu of cotton same as me. He always says don't put all your land in one crop. Wheat-maize double crop is our insurance — even if one fails, the other usually carries us through.

This year, I already planted my winter wheat last October on 8 mu. I bought improved seed from the seed station, about 30 jin total. I did rotary tillage before planting — everyone here does that. For the wheat, I'll irrigate four times: once before winter to help it survive the cold, once when it turns green in spring, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. I'll topdress with urea at jointing if the wheat looks yellow. Better to put a bit more fertilizer than risk a bad year — a poor harvest hurts more than wasting a few yuan on extra urea.

After wheat harvest in early June, there's almost no time — maybe five or six days before you have to get the maize in the ground, or you lose the growing season. So I'll plant summer maize right away, no-tillage, using Denghai hybrid seed. That's what my nephew uses and he gets good yields, around 1200 jin per mu sometimes. Maize doesn't need as much water as wheat, maybe irrigate twice if the summer is dry.

I also keep 2 mu for cotton. Cotton is more work — my wife helps with the spraying and picking. You have to spray for bollworm maybe 14 or 15 times through the season, and irrigate two or three times. But cotton prices have been okay, and it's cash in hand after the harvest.

For fertilizer, I don't calculate kilos exactly like the extension people do. I buy compound fertilizer by the bag — usually one bag per mu for wheat as base dressing, and another half bag for topdressing. For maize I put compound in the rows when planting. If you ask me in kilograms, I reckon it's about 15 kg nitrogen per mu for wheat, maybe 12 kg for maize, and about 10 kg for cotton. The compound fertilizer has some phosphorus and potassium in it too — maybe 5 or 6 kg phosphorus and 3 or 4 kg potassium per mu for the grains, a bit less for cotton.

I expect about 1000 jin per mu for wheat, 1100 jin for maize, and around 600 jin for cotton. That's what I usually get, and my neighbors get about the same.
